chunks: From him, from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Bakr al-Armani, who said:

I wrote to the Servant of God, peace be upon him, 'I am devoted to you. Indeed, I had dinars with a man, but he denied me. Then, dinars of his came into my possession. Should I take from under my hand what is owed to me? And if he swears an oath to me, I will swear that he has nothing against me.' He said, 'Yes, take from under your hand. And if he swears an oath to you, swear to him that he has nothing against you.'
And from him, from Abu Abdillah, from al-Husayn ibn Ali, from Abdillah ibn Waddah, who said:

There was a transaction between me and a Jew, and he cheated me of one thousand dirhams. I brought him before the governor, and I made him swear an oath, and he swore to me. And I knew that he swore to me a false oath. After that, he had many profits and dirhams. I wanted to take back the one thousand dirhams that were with him, which he had sworn about. So I wrote to Abu al-Hasan, peace be upon him, and informed him that I had made him swear and he had sworn, and that he had wealth with me. If you command me to take the one thousand dirhams he swore about, I will do so. He wrote to me, peace be upon him: 'Do not take anything from him. If he wronged you, do not wrong him. And if it were not for the fact that you accepted his oath and made him swear, I would have commanded you to take it from under your hand. But since you accepted his oath, the oath has passed with what is in it.' So I did not take anything from him, and I adhered to the letter of Abu al-Hasan, peace be upon him.

key_terms.ٱسْتَحْلَفَنِي: He asked me to swear / He made me swear

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on keeping a debtor's money if they swear an oath denying the debt?
ai.summary: These narrations from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidate the jurisprudential nuance of *al-yamin al-fajirah* (the perjurious oath) in debt recovery, distinguishing between cases where the creditor retains control of the debtor's assets versus those where the creditor voluntarily accepts the oath to settle the claim. The second hadith, attributed to Imam al-Kazim, highlights the Shia ethical principle of *la tazlimun* (do not wrong him) even when entitled to retribution, emphasizing that voluntary acceptance of the oath finalizes the transaction. This reflects the broader Shia legal tradition of balancing strict contractual rights with moral equity (*adl* and *ihsan*).
